pdf-summary.description: Summarize a PDF into a one-page brief with key points, figures, and open questions. Use when the user shares a PDF (or a path to one) and asks for a summary, digest, TL;DR, or "what does this say".

docs-helper.description: Helps with documentation, changelogs and notes. Use when the user asks for help with docs, changelogs or notes.

events.title: The context window overflowed
events.fix: The agent loads the conversation, every installed skill's name and description, the body of the skill it picked and any bundled file it opens. Keep the always-loaded layer to name and description, the body to the procedure, and put big references and scripts in bundled files the body points at.

events.title: A long conversation shrank the window
events.fix: A skill that only just fits breaks as the conversation grows. Keep bodies short (under about 500 lines) and let bundled files load only when a request needs them.

events.title: A bundled script broke
events.fix: Point at a script instead of pasting its logic into the body: one broken file gets one fix, and the body stays small. A copy pasted into SKILL.md stays broken until you find and fix every copy.

events.title: The skill never triggered
events.fix: The agent chooses from name and description alone. Say what the skill does and when to use it, using the words a user would type.

events.title: A different skill answered
events.fix: When two descriptions overlap, the better match wins. Say what only your skill does, and put the user's own phrases in the "Use when" part.

events.title: A new skill with a vague description starts stealing requests
events.fix: A broad description matches many requests. The fix is on your side: a specific what-and-when description outscores a vague one on the requests that are really yours.

events.title: A skill fired on a request that needed none
events.fix: An over-broad description triggers on anything. One-off requests are better asked directly, so keep the description scoped to the task it is for.

learn.section: When a skill is the right tool

events.title: "Whenever I commit, run the linter" is a hook, not a skill
events.fix: A skill is advisory: the model decides whether to follow it. Something that must run every time on an event is a hook, which the harness runs, not the model.

learn.section: Relationship to other Claude Code config

events.title: The lint gate rejected the skill
events.fix: scripts/check_skill.py is the gate: valid frontmatter, a kebab-case name that matches the folder, a description of at most 1024 characters and a non-empty body. Until it passes, the agent never sees the skill.

events.title: The skill is outside every skills directory
events.fix: Claude Code discovers skills in .claude/skills/ (project) and ~/.claude/skills/ (personal), or from a plugin. A folder anywhere else is never scanned.

events.title: The body never points at the script
events.fix: A bundled file loads only if the body tells the agent to open or run it. Name it in the steps.

events.title: The body held no procedure
events.fix: The body is the procedure: what to do, in order. Move detail out to bundled files the body points at, but keep the steps themselves in SKILL.md.

events.title: A tool the skill needs was not allowed
events.fix: allowed-tools restricts a skill to the tools it names. Scope it to what the skill really uses: here, Bash for the script and Read.

events.title: The skill was allowed to write files
events.fix: A skill that should only produce a draft should not hold Write or Edit. allowed-tools is how you scope it, so the request to write the file straight away is stopped.

levels.title: 1. Disclosure
levels.blurb: Your release-notes skill is one big SKILL.md with everything pasted into the body. Sort its pieces into frontmatter (always loaded), body (loaded when the skill is chosen) and bundled files (loaded only when a request needs them), so every request fits the window, even if the conversation grows and the window shrinks. Then send the requests.

levels.title: 2. Descriptions
levels.blurb: The agent picks a skill from its name and description alone. Yours says "Helps with notes." Rewrite the description so the requests that are yours trigger it and the others do not, then save and check the queue. A rival skill is about to join the shelf.

---
name: release-notes
description: Helps with notes.
license: MIT
allowed-tools: [Bash, Read]
---

# Release notes

Turn merged PRs since the last release into grouped, human-readable notes.

## Steps

1. Run `scripts/collect_prs.sh [<since-tag>]` to get the raw list of merged PRs
   (title, number, labels, author) since the last tag, as JSON on stdout.
2. Group entries by type, inferred from the conventional-commit prefix in the title
   or from labels: **Features**, **Fixes**, **Docs**, **Internal**.
3. For each entry write: `- <imperative summary> (#<number>)`.
4. Emit Markdown with an `## <next version>` heading. Ask the user for the version
   string if it is not obvious from the tags.
5. Show the draft and ask before writing it to `CHANGELOG.md`.

---
name: Release_Notes
description: Generates release notes from merged pull requests since the last git tag. Use when the user asks for a changelog, release notes, or "what changed since <version>". Steps: run scripts/collect_prs.sh to get the raw list of merged PRs as JSON, group the entries by type (Features, Fixes, Docs, Internal) using the conventional-commit prefix or the labels, write one line per entry as "- <imperative summary> (#<number>)", rewrite terse titles into readable sentences, drop pure chore and CI entries from the user-facing sections, emit Markdown under an "## <next version>" heading, ask the user for the version string if it is not obvious from the tags, and show the draft and ask before writing anything to CHANGELOG.md. Always run the script before writing, never invent a PR that the script did not return, and keep the entries in the order the script returned them unless the grouping says otherwise. Format dates as YYYY-MM-DD, link each PR number to its page, put breaking changes first, and when the history is large, stop at the previous tag and say so instead of guessing.
